claim: Non-parallel evolution does not preclude the possibility of selection.
source: Given that non-parallel evolution does not preclude the possibility of selection (Barghi et al., 2019; Barghi et al., 2020), there has been a sustained interest in elucidating the factors that influence the extent of genetic parallelism (i.e. how similar is the response of the same gene to selection in multiple populations from the same/similar ecological niche(s)) (Bolnick et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies supporting this claim.

claim: The degree of pleiotropy may be a potential factor associated with parallelism.
source: It has been proposed that the degree of pleiotropy, the number of traits affected by a single gene, maybe a potential factor associated with parallelism (Bolnick et al., 2018; Conte et al., 2015; Rennison and Peichel, 2022; Stern, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies proposing this relationship.

claim: New mutations in highly pleiotropic genes are more likely to have negative fitness effects than mutations in less pleiotropic genes.
source: New mutations in highly pleiotropic genes are more likely to have negative fitness effects than mutations in less pleiotropic genes as more traits are displaced from their optima.
evidence: The manuscript describes the cost of pleiotropy concept.

claim: The 'cost of pleiotropy' model is evidenced by the lack of sequence divergence observed in genes with a higher level of pleiotropy.
source: This 'cost of pleiotropy' model (Orr, 2000) is evidenced by the lack of sequence divergence observed in genes with a higher level of pleiotropy (Fraser et al., 2002; Hahn and Kern, 2005; Masalia et al., 2017; Josephs et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies supporting the cost of pleiotropy model.

claim: Less pleiotropic genes are more likely to contribute to adaptation over long evolutionary timescales.
source: Consequently, it can be postulated that less pleiotropic genes are more likely to contribute to adaptation over long evolutionary timescales, given that they have a higher probability of accumulating beneficial genetic variants.
evidence: The manuscript provides a logical inference from the cost of pleiotropy model.

claim: Less pleiotropic genes result in a more parallel selection response in different populations/species.
source: This results in a more parallel selection response in different populations/species (Hansen, 2003).

claim: The influence of pleiotropy on the selection response strongly depends on the genetic correlation of the affected traits and the underlying fitness function.
source: It has been proposed that the influence of pleiotropy on the selection response strongly depends on the genetic correlation of the affected traits and the underlying fitness function which connects phenotypic values with fitness (Blows, 2007; Lande and Arnold, 1983; Lande, 1979).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies proposing this relationship.

claim: Synergistic pleiotropy may result in stronger net selection and consequently in more parallel selection signatures.
source: If the fitness effects of the affected traits are positively correlated (synergistic pleiotropy), this may result in stronger net selection (Thorhölludottir et al., 2023) and consequently in more parallel selection signatures (MacPherson and Nuismer, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies supporting this claim.

claim: The correlation of fitness effects determines whether pleiotropy increases or decreases parallel selection signatures.
